The Ofﬁce assists United Nations Member States to establish legal and regulatory frameworks to govern space activities and strengthens the capacity of developing countries to use space science, technology and applications for development by helping to integrate space capabilities into national development programmes. Through the United Nations Programme on Space Applications, UNOOSA conducts international workshops, training courses and pilot projects on topics that include remote sensing, satellite navigation, satellite meteorology, tele-education and basic space sciences for the beneﬁt of developing nations. The International Committee on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (ICG) facilitates compatibility, interoperability and transparency between all the satellite navigation systems, to promote and protect the use of their open service applications and thereby beneﬁt the global community. UN-Space convenes annual sessions of the Inter-Agency Meeting on Outer Space Activities to discuss space-related matters among United Nations system entities. UN-Space organizes informal sessions that are open to Member States, private sector, non-governmental institutions and academia.
UNOOSA is also the United Nations focal point for satellite imagery requests during disasters and manages the United Nations Platform for Space-based Information for Disaster Management and Emergency Response (UN-SPIDER), established in 2006. The programme has the mandate to “ensure that all countries and international and regional organizations have access to and develop the capacity to use all types of space-based information to support the full disaster management cycle” .
Geospatial Data and Technology UNOOSA uses and promotes the use of free Earth observation data but is also a signatory to memoranda of understanding (MoUs) with providers of (geospatial) Earth observation data such as Airbus, DigitalGlobe/Maxar, China National Space Administration, and others in development. The satellite imagery is used for the monitoring of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), disaster risk reduction and monitoring of impacts of climate change. The Ofﬁce has access to additional Earth observation (EO) data and products through various mechanisms: as an authorized user, UNOOSA can trigger the International Charter “Space and Major Disasters” on request of government agencies; UNOOSA is a Joint Project Team member of Sentinel Asia and a user of the Copernicus EMS; it is also an active member of the International Working Group on Satellite-based Emergency Mapping (IWG-SEM) (http://www.un-spider.org/ network/iwg-sem). Geospatial Usage Geospatial data are used for disaster management and sustainable development purposes. UNOOSA promotes the use of geospatial data and tools through dedicated knowledge portals, such as the UN-SPIDER portal (http://www.un-spider.
org/), workshops and training sessions, mostly organized in countries of need. UN-SPIDER has a series of documented recommended practices that are available to practice step-by-step with satellite data in open-source geographic information system (GIS) software. UNOOSA connects data providers with data users and participates in the Group on Earth Observations (GEO) and Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) events. 19 SECRETARIAT UNOOSA Geospatial Resources UNOOSA has two remote sensing/GIS professional staff and a pool of interns/visiting scientists that work on geospatial information and remote sensing applications. Furthermore, UNOOSA has a network of six Regional Centres for Space, Science and Technology Education and an expanding network of twenty-three Regional Support Ofﬁces (RSOs) for UN-SPIDER. The RSOs have a large number of experts in geospatial information and remote sensing and work with Earth observation data (space agencies, research centres, universities or disaster management institutions) and use their expertise to assist countries in the use of data for emergency response and disaster management. The experts from the RSOs assist at training workshops, provide training material and provide maps and data analysis at all stages of the disaster management cycle. The scope of work is in line with ECA ’s mandate to support regional priorities and initiatives. The objective is to promote and expand the use of geospatial resources (data, information and services) in decision-making processes related to sustainable development, economic growth, natural resource management, environmental protection and social progress. Appropriate geospatial data and information should also be made available to the entire community of users.
Key geospatial activities include:  Developing and maintaining purpose-driven geospatial information resources, such as spatial data, standards and tools, to support regional initiatives. This aims to improve access to and use of spatially enabled data for informed decision-making in Africa’s development agenda.  Supporting the implementation, monitoring and evaluation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which require geospatial datasets for evidence-based decision-making.  Assisting Member States, subregional and regional institutions in developing and integrating spatial data infrastructures and integrated geospatial information frameworks at national and regional levels.  Strengthening the integration of statistics and geospatial information by mainstreaming geospatial technology into statistical processes.  Providing technical support to subprogrammes and ECA entities to incorporate geographic information systems (GIS), remote sensing and other geoinformation tools in analysing and presenting socioeconomic data for research and policy analysis.  Advancing comprehensive geospatial information policies that align with international programmes and initiatives, including the United Nations Global Geospatial Information Management (UN-GGIM), for which ECA serves as the Secretariat for UN-GGIM: Africa.  As Secretariat of UN-GGIM: Africa, the Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) also guides Member States in developing their policies, standards and institutional and legal frameworks through the development of policy guidelines and relevant frameworks. Examples of this work include:  Development of a policy guideline for the implementation of National Spatial Data Infrastructure (NSDI).  Supporting Member States in the development and implementation of their national spatial data infrastructures.  Supporting Member States in the development and implementation of their national action plan for integrated geospatial information frameworks.  Development of a geospatial data taxonomy for use in tracking the SDGs in Africa;  Assessment of the availability of geospatial datasets for monitoring and implementing the SDGs at the national level.  Development of a Geospatial and Statistical Framework for Africa to integrate geospatial and statistical information at regional and national levels. Geospatial Data and Technology ECA sources and manages socioeconomic data and data relevant for the monitoring of SDG indicators. It is continuously building regional geospatial databases: fundamental, core datasets and thematic data for various economic sectors. Some of the regional databases include: the African component of the Second Level Administrative Boundaries (SALB) geodatabase, which compiles authoritative administrative boundaries from National Geospatial Information Authorities and a regional infrastructure geodatabase. ECA also develops web-based applications using modern web technologies and services to enhance the integration, accessibility and usability of geospatial information and statistics. It employs platforms and systems such as ArcGIS Server, ArcGIS Online and image-analysis software (e.g., ERDAS Imagine) for data management and analysis. 23 REGIONAL COMMISSIONS ECA endeavours to research and demonstrate the use of emerging technologies such as artiﬁcial intelligence, machine learning and GeoAI. It also explores open-platforms, open data and open-source software and advises and encourages Member States to adopt these tools for their geospatial and statistical work.
Geospatial Usage At ECA, geospatial information is essential to:  Maintain ECA ’s role in supporting Member States to strengthen geospatial capacity and to serve as the regional anchor for intergovernmental proceedings.6  Stay current with global United Nations trends by placing equal emphasis on geospatial information management, in line with other regional commissions and Headquarters.  Maintain momentum in supporting ECA ’s constituencies by strengthening geospatial capacity in African countries and promoting its use to address key regional and global challenges.  Ensure harmonized geospatial methods and tools through interoperable data aligned with common frameworks and standards adopted at all levels.
In addition to these institutional roles, ECA uses geospatial data in its operations to support evidence-based policymaking, research and monitoring of the SDGs. As part of its think tank function, ECA conducts research and produces thematic publications and policy briefs that include maps and other geospatial products. Flagship publications include: Economic Report on Africa (ERA), Assessing Regional Integration in Africa (ARIA) and Africa Sustainable Development Report. One example of applied use is a prototype web application developed to demonstrate the integration of geospatial and statistical data for mapping and monitoring the SDGs. 24 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM Economic Commission for Europe (ECE) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) has no regular funding allocated for geospatial activities, therefore it has no geospatial posts and is not able to provide secretariat support to UN-GGIM: Europe. Activities are dependent on extrabudgetary funding sources. The UNECE Statistical Division participates in global and regional initiatives, including UN-GGIM, the European Forum for Geography and Statistics (EFGS) and the Geographic Information System of the Commission (GISCO). Every two years, the Conference of European Statisticians is organized back-to-back with the UN-GGIM: Europe meeting, featuring a joint day to strengthen collaboration.
Supported by European Union funding, the Statistical Division has initiated the Integration of Geospatial and Statistical Data (INGEST) project (2023-2024) to build capacity in integrating geospatial and statistical data. Under the INGEST project, the following activities were undertaken: 1. Set-up of the UNECE Task Force on Standards Issues for Integration of Statistical and Geospatial Information publication of: A path towards the use of common standards to support the Integration of Geospatial and Statistical information (UNECE 2024) and Issues and obstacles to the greater integration of statistical and geospatial information across the UNECE region (UNECE 2024). 2. Organization of a Joint UNECE, Eurostat, UN-GGIM: Europe Workshop on the Integration of Geospatial and Statistical Data, aimed at strengthening ties between statistical and geospatial communities across the UNECE region, promoting collaboration and advancing integration through institutional partnerships and the adoption of common standards.
3. Launch of the INGEST blog series, which explores a range of data integration topics and shares guidance, resources and best practices to support data integration efforts.
4. Capacity development in integrating geospatial and statistical data: • Integrate Assessment Tool v1.0 (UNECE 2024), designed to identify current and target maturity levels across a set of dimensions. • INGEST Maturity Assessment Tool v1.0 (UNECE 2024), to assess technical capabilities for data integration, focusing on data, technical infrastructure and standards. • Country studies on the integration of geospatial and statistical data in Albania, Armenia and Kazakhstan.
The UNECE Statistical Division plans to launch a second phase of the INGEST project in 2025, with funding from the European Commission (Eurostat).
Under the Inland Transport Committee of the UNECE Transport Division, the International Transport Infrastructure Observatory (ITIO) has been established. The observatory is an innovative example of how government data on new transport infrastructure projects can be presented to ﬁnancial institutions and other donors in a transparent, comprehensive and ‘bankable’ manner. It is designed as an online platform where (a) governments ﬁnd the data to prepare, benchmark and present their transport infrastructure projects and (b) ﬁnancial institutions can consider, analyse and compare projects from a regional and international perspective to identify opportunities for ﬁnancing.
The observatory is being developed on a geographic information system (GIS) platform that provides services to users, particularly governments and international ﬁnancial institutions. This United Nations GIS centre for transport infrastructure allows users to ﬁnd and analyse data on all transport networks and nodes (roads, railways, inland waterways, ports, airports, intermodal terminals, logistics centres and border crossing points), along with data on transport corridors (length, services, missing links, schedules and tariffs). It also includes data on new transport infrastructure projects, trafﬁc and cargo ﬂows and the ratiﬁcation and implementation of international conventions and agreements.

26 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) Geospatial Activities Since 2017 , the management of geospatial information has been systematically incorporated into the work agenda of the Statistics Division of the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC), reﬂecting its growing relevance and importance within the United Nations system. This signiﬁcance is demonstrated by the active functioning of the Committee of Experts on Global Geospatial Information Management (UN-GGIM), which reports directly to the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) and designates the authorities of Member States’ national geospatial agencies as focal points.
This Committee of Experts prepares and disseminates guidelines on various topics, including the integration of statistical and geospatial information, the use of geospatial information to support disaster management, geospatial support for the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, land administration, maritime affairs and other related matters.
In this context, ECLAC has served since 2021 as the Technical Secretariat of the United Nations Regional Committee on Global Geospatial Information Management for the Americas (UN-GGIM: Americas). ECLAC supports the Board of Directors of UN-GGIM: Americas in the formulation, execution and monitoring of geospatial capacity strengthening projects. It also facilitates the participation of Member States in global UN-GGIM working groups, provides technical support for regional and subregional geospatial events and offers technological support for the dissemination of geospatial and statistical information. At the national level, the Statistics Division provides technical assistance on geospatial matters through projects tailored to national priorities. This includes inter-institutional workshops and coordination with national statistical ofﬁces, national geospatial agencies and other relevant organizations, to strengthen governance, develop geospatial policies and promote international standards. It also supports the development and implementation of geospatial data systems and technological tools for managing and disseminating both geospatial and statistical information. Geospatial Data and Technology ECLAC is increasingly using geospatial data to support the production of information and knowledge across its substantive areas. In line with global United Nations guidelines on integrating geospatial and statistical information, new functionalities have been added to the Comisión Económica para América Latina y el Caribe Statistical Platform (CEPALSTAT) platform to link statistical data from various sources to speciﬁc locations, enabling the representation and dissemination of geospatial layers. To maximize the use and beneﬁt of this information, ECLAC has implemented an integrated and collaborative management model based on a corporate geospatial data infrastructure. This model incorporates standardized procedures for the maintenance, integration, analysis and use of geospatial data.
This collaborative work model is implemented through the ECLAC Geospatial Platform (CEPALGEO), which includes a suite of technological tools such as catalogues, viewers and geospatial services that allow remote discovery and access to geospatial information products from both internal and external sources. CEPALGEO applies standards and protocols to support data exchange, integration and interoperability within a broad regional and global data ecosystem.
Geospatial Usage ECLAC uses geospatial information to support its efforts in promoting economic and social development across the region. These datasets, organized by themes such as society, economy, environment and cross-cutting issues, are part of its core information assets.
Geospatial data are applied in a wide range of activities, including research projects, the design of public policy instruments, monitoring platforms and technical assistance.
Success stories include the Observatory on the Economic and Social Impact of COVID-19, the Interactive Map of Cluster Initiatives and Territorial Productive Articulation, Care Maps and studies on new concepts of rurality, among others.

” FUNDS, PROGRAMMES & RESEARCH 3 34 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is streamlining its geospatial activities under a uniﬁed strategy informed by its data strategy, aiming to enhance governance, standards, and tools for sustainable development. Geospatial efforts span crisis response, measurement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), biodiversity conservation, and policymaking in over 170 countries. UNDP is building a governance framework and technology stack to ensure initiatives comply with United Nations Geospatial Network standards and align with global agendas such as the Paris Agreement, and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
UNDP provides geographic information system (GIS) support organization-wide, harmonising decentralised GIS to reduce costs, boost data sharing, raise standards, and minimise redundancy. It maintains a GIS infrastructure, delivers training globally, and applies geospatial technologies across monitoring, disaster management, urbanisation, and recovery. Key projects include ﬂood prediction in South Sudan, GeoAI damage assessment in Gaza, Port-au-Prince, and Ukraine, storm analysis in Libya, landcover monitoring in Kosovo, and waste management in Guatemala. Partnerships, such as with UNOPS for mine risk monitoring and NASA-JPL for Ukraine recovery, further strengthen these efforts. Local GIS support from country ofﬁces underpins development work.
UNDP uses geospatial tools for biodiversity conservation and sustainable land management. The UN Biodiversity Lab (UNBL) is an open-source platform supporting national and international monitoring, reporting, and collaboration in line with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, helping countries track biodiversity and ecosystem health, integrate national data, and meet reporting requirements.
Geospatial Data and Technology UNDP collects, manages and uses a wide variety of geospatial data to inform decision-making and support development goals, leveraging both internal platforms and external datasets. The organization is also advancing its strategy for AI, including GeoAI, and open data.
Types of Geospatial Data Collected, Managed, or Used Examples of key data types include: satellite imagery and remote sensing data, geospatial vector and raster data, ground-truth data collection, real-time location and environmental data, socioeconomic data, biodiversity data. Data Management Platforms and Systems UNDP primarily relies on: Esri products and licenses, Google Earth Engine and Gemini, Microsoft Azure (Storage Blob, Managed PostgreSQL, Container Instances, Kubernetes Cluster, Web Apps, Service Bus), open-source platforms (QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, Python, PostGIS, Apache Arrow and GitHub) GeoAI and Open Data Strategy Through 2030 GeoAI: UNDP is strengthening its geospatial data analysis with GeoAI technologies. Newly published UNDP’s AI guidelines and policies will ensure responsible, ethical use of AI for improved decision-making, predictive modelling, visualising spatial trends, and disaster response.
Open Data: UNDP is dedicated to making geospatial data open, accessible, and easy to ﬁnd. Its Geospatial platforms use open data sources to improve analysis. Additionally, UNDP ensures that its own geospatial data can be easily shared. This approach supports UNDP’s commitment to transparency and advancing data-driven solutions for sustainable development. Access to commercial datasets is supported through the Development Data Partnership (https://datapartnership.org/). Open-Source Software: UNDP uses a hybrid geospatial approach, combining open-source GIS and proprietary solutions such as Esri, Google, and Microsoft products to enhance ﬂexibility and cut costs. This integration allows UNDP to meet diverse geospatial needs efﬁciently by leveraging both open-source innovation and advanced commercial tools.
Geospatial Usage Disaster Risk Reduction and Response UNDP uses geospatial data to support early warning systems, disaster response, and preparedness. This 35 FUNDS, PROGRAMMES AND RESEARCH approach supports improved relief strategies and resilience efforts. For instance, UNDP’s pilot project in Melitopol, Ukraine, helped assess building damage and inform recovery plans with actionable data. GeoAI has also aided damage evaluation in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, and Gaza, Palestine. Tools such as the Rapid Change Assessment Tool and GeoHub dynamic layers further support the UNDP Crisis Bureau.
Monitoring and Reporting Geospatial data is crucial for tracking the SDGs. UNDP employs spatial analysis to monitor key indicators and share results via story maps and dashboards. Examples include using geospatial data for SDG 7 to evaluate electricity access, and a GIS portal in Panama that tracks projects and partnerships for SDG 17 .
Monitoring and Evaluation Geospatial data enables UNDP to monitor projects in real or near-real time, track effectiveness, and make timely adjustments. Using GIS and satellite imagery, UNDP supports project monitoring and evaluation, ensuring accountability and effective implementation. For instance, in the Lake Chad Basin, UNDP’s two-phase stabilization project aims to reduce violence and support long-term peacebuilding in Cameroon, Chad, Niger, and Nigeria. An ArcGIS Site with webmaps and dashboards was developed to enhance monitoring and coordination among stakeholders.
Geospatial Resources UNDP’s geospatial capability is decentralised with teams across country ofﬁces, regional bureaus and central bureaus, but with strong collaboration between them and a focus on the utilization of corporate UNDP tools. Core platforms include ESRI products and licenses, Google Earth Engine, Microsoft Azure (Storage Blob, Managed PostgreSQL), Azure Container Instances, Azure Kubernetes Cluster, Azure Web App, Azure Service Bus) and open-source platforms (e.g., QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, Python, PostGIS, Apache Arrow). 38 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA)’s mission is to deliver a world where every pregnancy is wanted, every childbirth is safe and every young person’s potential is fulﬁlled. UNFPA relies extensively on census and survey data collected across countries to assess progress and remains a key partner to National Statistical Ofﬁces in generating and analysing high-quality population data. The 2020 Census Round has seen a growing use of, and demand for, geospatial technologies to ensure data quality, identify vulnerable populations, improve resource allocation and strengthen evidence-based decision-making.
Within UNFPA ’s Programme Division, the Data, Demography and Development Branch (DDDB) has been mandated by the organization’s leadership to expand the use of geospatial data and to support the UNFPA Strategic Plan. This dedicated branch spearheads the integration of geospatial science and data-driven approaches across UNFPA ’s programmatic areas. In this regard, a range of impactful geospatial initiatives has been undertaken:  Enhancement and maintenance of the UNFPA Population Data Portal, integrating geospatial data from multiple sources to monitor key indicators across gender, health and broader population and development domains.  Support to the modernization of the 2020 Census Round in data collection, utilization and dissemination, including the incorporation of geographic information system (GIS) in census cartography, the use of GIS and satellite imagery to enhance data quality and coverage and the generation of geospatial census datasets.  Supporting countries in using population data to map geospatial inequalities and advance “leaving no one behind” , including mapping geographic access to essential sexual and reproductive health services.  Collaboration with partners to produce high-resolution population estimates in hard-to-reach areas, providing vital data for humanitarian response.  Joint Programme support to countries in strengthening national capacities to generate urban and rural statistics using the standardized Degree of Urbanization methodology, enabling globally comparable statistics and SDG monitoring, in partnership with EC-JRC, UN-Habitat, United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD) and United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF).  Mapping global population exposure and vulnerability to climate change by integrating population data, census and household survey data with climate change and diverse spatial datasets.  Development of small-area estimation methods using census, survey and geospatial data to estimate family planning indicators at the small administrative unit level.

42 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) uses geospatial tools to strengthen data-driven decision-making, improve emergency preparedness and response, and support global development priorities, including the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Geospatial analysis informs climate resilience by assessing risks, monitoring environmental change and guiding adaptive measures. In emergencies, it enables rapid mapping of impacts, access, partner activities and infrastructure damage to direct resources where most needed. The Data and Analytics Section coordinates geospatial support for major crises, including Ukraine, Gaza and Lebanon, working closely with Country Ofﬁces to address local challenges. Across development programmes, geospatial insights help target poverty reduction and improve access to essential services, optimizing the impact of investments. With partners, UNICEF supports geo-enabled microplanning for health services and strengthens government capacity to manage core geospatial data and apply spatial analysis in health programming. Spatial analysis is integral to the MICS programme, enhancing the precision and usability of socioeconomic data collected through household surveys.
Geospatial Data and Technology UNICEF uses a wide range of geospatial data to support its diverse applications, relying on partners and open data providers to ensure global spatial datasets are integrated into internal processes. Commonly used datasets include subnational administrative boundaries, statistical indicators, facility locations (schools, health centres), population data (including high-resolution rasters), infrastructure layers (roads, ports, border crossings) and Earth observation data and derived products for climate and environmental analysis. The climate analytics team has been using Google Earth Engine and its resources to generate high-resolution child hazard data and has tested GeoAI applications to enable map-based chatbot querying that combines indicator and hazard data within a single interface.
At a corporate level, UNICEF employs a hybrid geospatial architecture that combines proprietary tools (primarily Esri) with open-source solutions. UNICEF is an active contributor to the Digital Public Goods Alliance and is developing and maintaining corporate open-source platforms such as GeoRepo, which provides harmonized administrative boundaries and core datasets, and GeoSight, which enables visualisation of subnational indicators and spatial layers. Additional open-source tools support speciﬁc use cases, for example the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS) Geocode Plugin for QGIS for anonymizing survey cluster locations and AccessMod 5 for modelling physical accessibility to health services.
Most of UNICEF’s spatial datasets are stored in its corporate web geographic information system (GIS) platforms, including ArcGIS Online, ArcGIS Enterprise and GeoSight, with harmonized global, subnational administrative boundaries stored in the GeoRepo platform and accessible through APIs and as vector tiles. UNICEF integrates Statistical Data and Metadata eXchange (SDMX) data standards and APIs to link the Data Warehouse with GeoRepo and GeoSight, improving interoperability and automation of data pipelines, including through GitHub, Databricks and Google Earth Engine.
UNICEF is also advancing the use of SDMX as a standard for disseminating indicator data and is actively building integrations between the SDMX indicator data warehouse and geospatial platforms to ensure that statistical data can be easily mapped and visualised. Open data, open software, open standards and the responsible use of GeoAI are likely to remain key principles for guiding the future use of geospatial technology at UNICEF . Geospatial Data and Technology WFP’s services are supported by a geospatial infrastructure and tools powered by both open-source and proprietary software to:  Automate the ingestion of global climate and Earth observation (EO) data and indicators  Apply cloud computing, geostatistics and machine learning for spatial analysis  Deliver high-value geospatial products for planning, implementation and emergency response  Provide user-friendly access to climate hazard and vulnerability data through interactive dashboards  Manage standardized global geographic reference data across operations The Humanitarian Data Cube (HDC) is central to the geospatial infrastructure, providing climate and Earth observation data and indicators to support WFP , governments and humanitarian partners globally.
PRISM is a tool developed in collaboration with governments and WFP country ofﬁces. It integrates real-time hazard data (such as droughts, ﬂoods, storms and earthquakes) with food security and socioeconomic vulnerability data to support early warning, anticipatory action and response planning. PRISM is recognized as a Digital Public Good.
Geospatial Usage Support to livelihoods and resilience programmes Geospatial tools and EO data are applied to design, monitor and evaluate resilience programmes:  Asset Impact Monitoring from Space (AIMS): Assesses long-term impacts of resilience interventions (e.g., reforestation, terracing) using satellite imagery, ensuring programmes are accountable, measurable and adaptive.  Integrated Context Analysis (ICA): Combines hazard and historical food security data to inform programme design.  Climate analysis: Uses historical and projected data to understand climate impacts on food security and inform resilience strategies that reduce risk and enhance adaptive capacity.
Support to emergency operations (preparedness and response) Geospatial analytics and early warning tools enhance emergency response:  Advanced Disaster Analysis and Mapping (ADAM): Delivers near real-time alerts and disaster impact assessments (e.g., ﬂoods, cyclones, earthquakes) to guide timely and targeted humanitarian actions.  Natural hazard risk analysis: Identiﬁes high-risk areas such as ﬂoods, storms and droughts to support preparedness and planning.  Emergency mapping and analysis: Produces maps and analytics on displacement, conﬂict zones, crop conditions and infrastructure damage to support situational awareness and operational decisions.
Seasonal monitoring and climate risk applications Geospatial tools support anticipatory action and risk reduction:  Seasonal monitoring and outlooks: analyse near real-time and forecast data on droughts, ﬂoods and temperature extremes to guide contingency planning.  Trigger models for anticipatory action: Develop data-driven triggers based on seasonal forecasts to enable preventive action ahead of hazards.  Strengthening national institutions: Builds the capacity of national agencies in forecasting and monitoring climate hazards through training, tools and data access.

46 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT), part of the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR), is a technology-intensive programme supporting the United Nations core objectives. As a centre of excellence for satellite imagery analysis and geographic information system (GIS) solutions, it provides geographic insight for senior decision-makers and ﬁeld workers within and outside the UN system, with special focus on Member States. UNOSAT is hosted at CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research. The vision of UNITAR-UNOSAT is to promote evidence-based decision-making for peace, security and resilience and its mission is to provide coordinated geospatial analysis and build capacities for the use of geoinformation technology towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The strategic objectives are to:  provide coordinated geospatial analysis to the United Nations and Member States in times of crisis,  develop capacities in the use of technology towards achieving the SDGs, and  develop and promote innovative geospatial solutions for the United Nations system, its partners and Member States.
These objectives result in geospatial products and services, primarily derived from satellite imagery, for decision-makers and ﬁeld personnel within Member States and the United Nations system, as well as capacity building of national and regional actors in the use of geographic information technologies (GIT) for disaster risk reduction, sustainable development, peace and security. Typical areas of satellite imagery analysis include humanitarian relief, conﬂict analysis, environmental assessments, protection of cultural heritage, disaster risk reduction and climate resilience, human rights and sustainable development. Knowledge transfer through training and capacity development for Member States and other actors is also provided within the same thematic areas. UNOSAT serves as the focal point for geospatial activities in the Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System (GDACS), coordinated by the United Nations Ofﬁce for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), including the Satellite Mapping Coordination System (SMCS), which facilitates operational coordination of satellite mapping activities during humanitarian disasters. UNOSAT also works with partners to develop artiﬁcial intelligence models for analysing satellite imagery and extracting useful vector data.
Structure UNOSAT consists of three sections:  Disaster Risk Management and Climate Resilience Section  Human Security and Human Rights Section  Business Exploration, Strategic Planning and Coordination Section UNOSAT has its headquarters in Geneva, with ofﬁces in Bangkok, Nairobi and New York. Geospatial Data and Technology UNOSAT focuses on satellite imagery from free and open-source and commercial data, in-kind donations and from the International Charter on Space and Major Disasters. It produces derived information products from satellite imagery and related geodata, including maps, statistics, reports and geodata for direct integration in GIS systems, as well as web maps, story maps and customised products. Many of these products are available via the UNOSAT website and the Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX), covering themes such as building damage, refugee settlements, ﬂood water extents and more.
Geospatial Usage Geospatial data from UNOSAT is used widely in support of Member States and United Nations entities with thematic mandates, along with the Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, the International Criminal Court and other organizations.

UNOPS delivers technical expertise, operational platforms and advisory support to a wide range of United Nations missions and national authorities, often in high-risk and post-conﬂict settings. IMAT leads geospatial innovation within UNOPS, developing practical tools with leading research institutions such as the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) and Carnegie Mellon University to assess infrastructure damage, prioritize recovery and monitor delivery in fragile and crisis-affected contexts.
Key Geospatial Functions:  Infrastructure damage assessments: UNOPS conducts infrastructure damage assessments through integrated satellite, geographic information system (GIS) and AI approaches, combining pre- and post-disaster imagery, change detection and AI classiﬁcation to quantify physical damage, prioritize redevelopment and inform recovery proposals.  Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)-linked spatial analysis: UNOPS performs this analysis across its projects and development needs to guide investment targeting in least developed countries and fragile states.  Risk estimation of explosive ordnance (EO): Using AI models and data from the EO sector and the Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX), UNOPS estimates the risk of EO to support humanitarian mine action prioritization and socioeconomic impact assessments. UNOPS has developed an AI-driven spatial analysis model for Myanmar mine action prioritization to identify high-risk areas based on population exposure and access constraints. A machine learning-based model for Afghanistan estimates landmine contamination in non-surveyed areas.  Integrated spatial dashboards: UNOPS uses integrated spatial dashboards for planning, monitoring and reporting, which include contract quality monitoring dashboards that integrate contract data with geospatial outputs to improve accountability and ﬁeld delivery.  Capacity-building: UNOPS provides capacity-building for partners in ﬁeld-based GIS and remote sensing, including training for government and UN partners such as the United Nations Mine Action Service (UNMAS), the United Nations Ofﬁce of Counter-Terrorism (UNOCT) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). Geospatial Data and Technology UNOPS has built a suite of cloud-native tools that process and visualise spatial data across operational contexts, often in collaboration with national actors and ﬁeld teams. Key systems and data types include:  UNOPS Infrastructure Monitoring Toolkit: This toolkit aggregates global disaster alerts (e.g., GDACS, NASA) and analyses them alongside UNOPS assets and past projects to guide response and investment.  Damage Assessment Framework: This framework combines pre- and post-disaster imagery, change detection and AI classiﬁcation to quantify physical damage, prioritize redevelopment and inform recovery proposals.  Spatial Dashboards: Dashboards integrate contract data with geospatial outputs to improve accountability and ﬁeld delivery. Examples include the Gaza Mine Action prioritization mapping application, which provides real-time access to relevant decision-making data for explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) ofﬁcers and the UNMAS UN GeoPortal IED Dashboard for reporting and analysis of mine action activities across multiple country programs.  RELand (Risk Estimation of Landmines): An AI-based system that uses HDX, ACLED and remote sensing data to spatially estimate EO risk for planning and prioritization. Developed with Carnegie Mellon University, it estimates the probability of EO contamination in a given hazard polygon to identify priority areas for mine action interventions in Afghanistan and globally.  Project Document Analysis App (PDAA): This application uses Large Language Models (LLMs) and geospatial embeddings to extract SDG relevance, indicators, 55 FUNDS, PROGRAMMES AND RESEARCH UNOPS remote sensing techniques and spatial planning elements from UNOPS documents. UNOPS is exploring the expansion of generative AI (GenAI) to automate business and operational processes.
IMAT tools rely on Google Cloud (Vertex AI, Earth Engine, BigQuery), Esri Enterprise, PostGIS and open-source stacks such as Leaﬂet.
Geospatial Usage UNOPS PSC IMAT’s geospatial tools are actively used in:  Emergency response and infrastructure recovery planning: For example, post-Hurricane Beryl in the Caribbean, IMAT deployed a full-stack AI and GIS system to rapidly identify, assess and propose reconstruction projects in disaster-affected areas.  SDG analysis and investment targeting: Particularly in least developed countries and fragile states. In Afghanistan, AI models are used to detect and measure positive socioeconomic changes resulting from humanitarian mine action activities, providing measurable indicators that directly contribute to the United Nations SDGs.  Humanitarian mine action prioritization and socioeconomic impact assessments: This includes the use of automated data-sharing protocols for comprehensive operational planning in Gaza.  National infrastructure master planning and project resilience assessments. In Syria, 3D models of rubble are created from stereo imagery to help inform planning and prioritization, aiding in debris assessment and safe removal operations.  Field-level training and capacity-building for government and United Nations partners.  IMAT also supports the development of global standard operating procedures (SOPs) for disaster damage assessment and redevelopment, combining AI, remote sensing and GIS for scalable response planning.

The team comprises GIS and remote sensing specialists, AI/ML engineers, full-stack developers, geospatial project managers and ﬁeld-based GIS advisors embedded in UNOPS projects. ” SPECIALIZED AGENCIES 4 60 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Geospatial Activities The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations that leads international efforts to defeat hunger. With 195 members (194 countries and the European Union) FAO has worked since 1945 in over 130 countries worldwide. Headquartered in Rome, Italy, FAO is present in over 130 countries. Article 1 of its constitution requires FAO to “collect, analyse, interpret and disseminate information related to nutrition, food and agriculture” . Given the inherent spatial dimension of agricultural activities, geospatial solutions are a critical enabler for the Organization to achieve its mandate and support its Members in the transformation to more efﬁcient, inclusive, resilient and sustainable agrifood systems. FAO, as a custodian agency of twenty-one indicators across six Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), supports its Members in data collection and reporting, including using geospatial tools. This is done through direct measurements, for example, of forest cover, land use changes or water consumption in agriculture, by supporting survey design and the disaggregation of data at the subnational level to inform decision-making processes. Geospatial Data and Technology Georeferenced data and information are collected and used across FAO departments and decentralised ofﬁces worldwide. The FAO agro-informatics platform integrates information technology with earth observation, remote sensing, agricultural data management, analysis and application to deliver reliable, timely, high-resolution, documented, integrated location-based information and analysis across diverse sectors and various sources. The platform includes FAO’s catalogue of geospatial data. The default FAO data license is Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). The platform is built on open-source technologies and is a digital public good. Initially designed to support the Hand-in-Hand Initiative, it has grown to become a powerful tool for delivering FAO’s work and achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 2 (Zero Hunger). It underpins many FAO applications catering to speciﬁc thematic and regional communities, including market-based transformation of agrifood systems, water data, animal disease management, climate-smart agriculture, crop production early warning, ecosystem restoration, globally federated integrated soil data, land cover, crop type mapping, crop calendar, phenology and smallholder advisory services. The platform offers rich data exploration features, including search and explore, time-series analysis, data comparison across locations and periods, visualisation, geospatial analysis, reports and stories. The platform has a thriving community with rapid growth in users and data. Currently, 175,000 users from 186 countries generate approximately twenty billion requests across two million layers and 5,000 datasets federated from one hundred organizations. 61 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES Geospatial Resources Geospatial applications are widely adopted in FAO for monitoring food security and agriculture, including forestry, ﬁshery and across disciplines, including socioeconomic and statistical domains. The Geospatial Unit in the Land and Water Division includes three staff and seventeen consultants, while the Agro-Informatics team in the IT Division includes four staff and twelve consultants. Other geospatial hubs with specialised skills are hosted in other departments and divisions, including Forestry, Fishery and Economy Departments and the Ofﬁce of Climate Change. Including regional and country ofﬁces, there are more than twenty-ﬁve staff and one hundred consultants worldwide. The Organization has developed and maintains a wide range of geospatial tools, including land cover metalanguage and classiﬁcation standards, cloud-based image analysis processing for forest resources monitoring, crop suitability and production assessment, livestock environmental assessment models, early warning for agricultural droughts and many more. Its easy-to-use interface, powered by cloud-based supercomputers, offers unparalleled satellite data access, supporting improved climate change mitigation and data-driven land-use policies. 62 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Geospatial Activities The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations, headquartered in Montreal, Canada, with seven regional ofﬁces worldwide (Bangkok, Cairo, Dakar, Lima, Mexico, Nairobi and Paris). It was established by Member States in 1944 to administer and govern the Convention on International Civil Aviation (commonly referred to as the “Chicago Convention”). ICAO serves as the global forum for States on international civil aviation. It develops global Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs), including guidance material, conducts safety oversight and compliance audits, performs studies and analyses of the air transport market, provides technical assistance to Member States and builds aviation capacity through cooperation among its Member States and stakeholders. ICAO maintains several geospatial datasets related to aviation, including but not limited to, lists of airports used for international civil aviation (location indicators), airport safety characteristics, airspace delineation, aviation routes and ﬁve-letter name codes for the identiﬁcation of signiﬁcant points and designators for air trafﬁc service (ATS) routes. ICAO maintains an aeronautical geographic information system (GIS) function within the Air Navigation Bureau (ANB) which responds to requests for maps and other geospatial services, including regional air navigation plans, crisis response and contingency mapping for situations affecting or involving civil aviation and geospatial analysis such as air trafﬁc growth, emissions estimation based on known trafﬁc schedules and performance measurements of regional and global civil aviation. 64 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) Geospatial Activities The International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) is an international ﬁnancial institution and a specialised agency of the United Nations, based in Rome, Italy. IFAD provides ﬁnancial resources to national governments for agricultural programmes that promote rural development. There are two main ways in which geospatial data and technology are used at IFAD:  Design of country strategies and investment projects, where geospatial information is used to identify vulnerable communities and areas in which the Fund wishes to invest.  Monitoring and impact evaluation, where location-speciﬁc data on investments and smallholders is collected during project implementation and completion. This data are used to monitor project progress and assess impact.
Geospatial Data and Technology IFAD’s design and evaluation teams use a wide range of external geospatial datasets to inform project design and assess impact. These include administrative boundaries, environmental, climate and socioeconomic datasets from a variety of providers. To manage and analyse these data, geographic information system (GIS) analysts at IFAD primarily use QGIS and ArcGIS platforms.
IFAD manages two types of geodata related to its operations. First, it produces a map for each project showing the administrative areas in which the project operates. These maps are also the basis on which IFAD reports the locations of its projects to the International Aid Transparency Initiative (IATI). Second, IFAD is increasingly collecting investment-level data, such as the location of markets, irrigation schemes or rural roads in which the Fund invests. This data is used for monitoring, impact evaluation and other operational purposes.
IFAD has developed an internal repository for geospatial data based on open-source technologies, including PostgreSQL/ PostGIS, GeoServer, Geonode and OpenLayers. It provides web-map and web dashboard functionality. IFAD users can store and access GIS ﬁles in different formats. IFAD has also developed an innovative GIS data delivery application called GeoScan, which provides access to over 180 different layers from major data providers. In addition, IFAD has developed a custom widget solution to integrate large volumes of geospatial data into Microsoft Power BI applications.
The Fund is currently developing a mobile application to collect and verify georeferenced ﬁeld-level data from its operations, enabling deeper insights into its impact on rural poverty and the environment.
IFAD has an in-house artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) development platform that combines many technologies to support multiple use cases, from machine learning for advanced analytics to generative AI for knowledge management. IFAD has several open-source projects available on platforms such as GitHub, incorporating contributions to and from open-source communities and developers.
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and IFAD are jointly developing the Adaptation, Biodiversity and Carbon Mapping (ABC-Map) tool, a geospatial application for analysing adaptation, biodiversity, land-use change and carbon.
The Fund is expected to award a grant to a public foundation to compile spatial, satellite-derived datasets on a wide range of topics for use in project design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation and impact assessment. These datasets will be publicly available.
IFAD is ﬁnancing a project (CAPEO) with the OpenGeoHub Foundation to compile spatial, satellite-derived datasets on a wide range of topics for use in project design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation and impact assessment, in partnership with Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP). These datasets will be publicly available. Geospatial Usage IFAD is committed to the systematic use of geospatial data and technologies in its operations to make evidence-based decisions and assess the impact of project activities, 65 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES particularly in land-based investments such as irrigation scheme development or rangeland rehabilitation. Geographic targeting and vulnerability assessment to identify vulnerable communities and areas where a project should intervene 2. The ILO became the ﬁrst specialized agency of the United Nations in 1946. The main aims of the ILO are to promote rights at work, encourage decent employment opportunities, enhance social protection and strengthen dialogue on work-related issues. As the only tripartite UN agency, the ILO brings together governments, employers and workers of 187 Member States to set labour standards, develop policies and design programmes promoting decent work for all women and men.
The ILO conducts geospatial activities, primarily through the STRENGTHEN2 project (Employment Impact Assessment to Maximize Job Creation in Africa). Co-ﬁnanced by the European Union, the project aims to assess the employment impacts of infrastructure investments in sub-Saharan Africa. It applies a range of methods to estimate both direct and indirect employment effects of projects. To assess the long-term impacts of investments, the ILO uses geographic information system (GIS) and remote sensing to measure the economic and employment effects of infrastructure and agricultural projects. Assessments using these geospatial methods have been conducted in Rwanda, Kenya, Zambia and Malawi. Beyond this, additional work on impact assessment within the ILO Employment Policy Department utilises spatial data to analyse the impacts of natural disasters, conﬂicts, labour productivity and inequality. The ILO’s 2025 Reference Guide on Employment Impact Assessment highlights GIS and remote sensing as increasingly essential tools for conducting Employment Impact Assessments (EmpIAs).
Georeferenced information is also disseminated through reports and dashboards, primarily via ILOSTAT , the ILO’s central portal for labour statistics. The ILO also compiles and makes available legal databases comprising labour laws, standards and policies from all Member States. These resources are often georeferenced and disseminated through reports, dynamic web pages and dashboards. Finally, multiple departments and ofﬁces collect a range of quality and impact indicators from programmes and projects worldwide. These are presented through dashboards that provide information on ILO development cooperation spending (DC Dashboard) across the globe, the evaluation process (i-eval Discovery) and the results achieved (IR Dashboard).
Geospatial Data and Technology The work on employment impact assessment utilises a range of geospatial and survey data:  Survey data: Census, household surveys and labour force surveys collect administrative data to produce national statistics on employment and shed light on the structure of the labour force. Labour force surveys, usually collected from a sample of individuals that are nationally representative, aim to capture the number of jobs and the characteristics of these jobs. This information can be used to track progress and for monitoring and planning purposes.  Satellite imagery: The use of satellite images in combination with algorithms can be used to monitor and evaluate projects over time.  Night-time lights satellite data: Night-light data are the amount of light at night that can be observed from outer space. Based on previous research, this can be applied as a proxy for GDP at the local level. This is particularly valuable in countries with under-resourced statistical systems.
Geospatial Usage GIS is applied under the STRENGTHEN2 project and within the Employment Policy Department to conduct the following analyses:  Night-time lights analysis to assess the impacts of transport projects, conﬂicts, natural disasters and inequality. Changes in light intensity before and after an event or project are analysed as a proxy for economic activity (GDP), which can be translated into estimated changes in employment at the local level and over time.  Labour force survey integration, combining employment information with geographic data, enables analysis of changes in employment outcomes before and International Labour Organization (ILO) 67 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES after project completion. STRENGTHEN2 applies this approach to assess the employment impacts of roads and agricultural projects, using a difference-in-differences econometric approach.  Satellite data analysis is used to monitor land-use change and agricultural productivity. Environmental indices derived from satellite imagery can be compared over time to assess the severity of events such as droughts or the impacts of irrigation schemes. This information is combined with survey data to assess impacts on jobs and livelihoods.  Accessibility analysis, using GIS, evaluates how road projects have improved access to services, such as education, health and markets, which in turn can support positive employment outcomes.
In addition to the STRENGTHEN2 project, the ILO has established a Geospatial Services Hub to provide access to geospatial data, cartography and mapping services for internal users. The Hub supports the production of ofﬁcial maps for all ILO publications, based on the latest version of the United Nations global cartography.
Geospatial Resources The ILO has dedicated resources for geospatial activities under the STRENGTHEN2 project, including a staff GIS specialist responsible for coordinating the GIS work. Additional colleagues within the Employment Policy Department also use geospatial data in their work. More broadly, specialists at headquarters and in ﬁeld ofﬁces contribute to the design and production of choropleth maps and other map-based visualisations. Field ofﬁces also support Member States in systematising georeferenced information to support the production of reports.

It also establishes requirements for search and rescue (SAR), the Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS), Long-range Identiﬁcation and Tracking (LRIT) and Electronic Chart Display and Information Systems (ECDIS).  Digital maritime information. With the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO) and other standards bodies, IMO supports e-navigation, application of S-100 standards in ECDIS, interoperable digital maritime services and alignment between S-100 and the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business.  Marine environmental protection. Geospatial Data & Technologies IMO instruments and reporting systems encompass geospatially referenced information including ship routeing measures and reporting-system limits; SAR regions and rescue coordination centres; GMDSS facilities; Particularly Sensitive Sea Areas (PSSAs) and MARPOL Special Areas; port reception facilities; casualty and piracy incident locations; dumping-site information; and LRIT ship-position information. Much of this information is submitted by Member States or Contracting Parties under IMO instruments and reporting procedures. Access to LRIT information is governed by SOLAS and the related LRIT technical documentation.
Core platforms and standards. The Global Integrated Shipping Information System (GISIS) is IMO’s comprehensive online hub for collecting, processing and sharing shipping-related data, with publicly accessible and restricted-access modules. LRIT provides global identiﬁcation and tracking of ships, supported by technical speciﬁcations covering data security and information exchange. IMO works with IHO on S-100 in ECDIS and e-navigation, while the IMO Compendium supports harmonized and interoperable exchange between ships, ports, Maritime Single Windows and public authorities.
Direction. IMO is upgrading GISIS following analysis of current operations and future data-management needs. Related work includes application of S-100 in ECDIS, an IP-based S-100 data-distribution framework, continued development of the IMO Compendium and further development of the IMO Strategy on Maritime Digitalization.
Geospatial Usage Geospatial information deﬁnes where maritime requirements and protective measures apply; supports voyage planning, navigation, distress communication and SAR coordination; and informs analysis, regulatory proposals and impact assessments. IMO-adopted geographic measures are published in IMO instruments and incorporated, as appropriate, into ofﬁcial charts and digital navigation products by national hydrographic authorities.

The ITU Secretariat is composed of a General Secretariat and three bureaus: the Radiocommunication Bureau (BR), the Development Bureau (BDT) and the Standardization Bureau (TSB). The ITU does not currently have a geospatial section or department. However, several staff in ITU, from different bureaus, work with geospatial data, both as developers and users. 72 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM United Nations Educational, Scientifc and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Geospatial Activities Created on 16 November 1945, the United Nations Educational, Scientiﬁc and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) is the United Nations’ organization for education, the sciences and culture. Its Constitution, drafted in the aftermath of World War II, opens with the following words, a road map for the Organization: “Since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed” . More than 70 years after UNESCO’s foundation, this vision of peace remains deeply relevant. It is, moreover, an essential condition for achieving sustainable development. UNESCO fosters dialogue and mutual understanding between peoples through education, the sharing of different cultures and the free circulation of ideas and knowledge.
Because of its complex mandate, UNESCO operates in multiple areas of geospatial activity, in relation to education, culture, sciences, freedom of expression and access to information. Approximately 10 million square kilometres of the Earth’s surface are now protected by UNESCO designated sites such as Biosphere Reserves, Global Geoparks and World Heritage sites and thousands of items inscribed in lists are geo-localized.
For example, some of the activities within the culture sector involve satellite monitoring of World Heritage properties to support the monitoring of these sites, enabling local authorities to identify potential threats, such as land use changes, which could place the sites in danger and thereby provide sufﬁcient time for authorities to develop and implement mitigation strategies. The World Heritage Online Map Platform represents a geodatabase of all 1,000+ World Heritage properties with near real-time monitoring. These data are then overlapped with data from other programs such as the Man and the Biosphere and the UNESCO Geoparks Network. Such tools directly contribute to the implementation of the 2030 Agenda, in particular to the achievement of Goal 11, Target 11.4: “Strengthen efforts to protect and safeguard the world’s cultural and natural heritage” .
Other important ongoing projects dedicated to the collection of geographical information are the International Hydrological Programme (IHP) Water Information Network System (WINS) online platform, an open-access online library and networking hub. For water, the UNESCO Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission Tsunami Programme also maintains the Tsunami Early Warning Systems (EWS) and is part of a global initiative that aims to build a complete map of the ocean ﬂoor by 2030.
Furthermore, UNESCO recently joined forces with the European Union (EU) community of scientists and practitioners to develop innovative solutions for strengthening resilience, via the development of several ICT platforms.
Geospatial Data and Technology While UNESCO applies and endorses open data policies whenever possible, it does not yet provide a single place where all geospatial-related data can be accessed. Each project provides its own data access policy. This is the case for the above mentioned projects and others. For example, the Landslide-EVO (Environmental Virtual Observatory) project, an international collaborative research initiative that demonstrated how the use of citizen science and advanced low-cost ICTs helped to develop a demand-responsive framework for landslide disaster risk reduction in the Karnali River Basin of Western Nepal, has developed participatory methods for augmenting geospatial hydrometeorological datasets in the mountains. The World Network of Biosphere Reserves holds the georeferenced data of all biosphere reserves and the Ibero-American and Caribbean Biosphere Reserves Network (IberoMAB) has the shapeﬁles of all its afﬁliated biosphere reserves. The same information is available for the 241 UNESCO Global Geoparks items.
The World Heritage Centre collects, produces, veriﬁes and manages vector layers reﬂecting the boundaries and buffer zones of World Heritage properties and speciﬁc datasets on threats to properties, including daily active ﬁres detected by VIIRS sensors (NASA) and recent earthquake data from the PAGER system.
Geospatial data collection is being used to inform emergency planning and management of natural hazards and disasters with the UNESCO G-WADI Geoserver application, which uses an artiﬁcial neural network algorithm to estimate real-time precipitation worldwide.
73 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES Some other UNESCO initiatives neither collect nor publish their own georeferenced data, as geospatial data are often provided by national authorities with restrictions. In the ﬁeld of education, for example, geospatial data on schools comes mainly from the ministries of education; cartographic and spatial data layers are obtained mainly from free database platforms; at the end of the process, georeferenced educational data are made available on the UNESCO website and on other different specialised platforms such as the Ofﬁce for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX), Armed Conﬂict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), International Organization for Migration Displacement Tracking Matrix (IOM–DTM), United States Geological Survey (USGS), NASA and United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP).
Geospatial Usage UNESCO makes use of geospatial data in a number of different areas. For education, for example, geospatial information is used at the International Institute for Educational Planning for micro-planning and school mapping in Member States, for climate risk and vulnerability analyses in crisis-sensitive planning and for supporting policy dialogue, including between host and refugee communities.
In culture, geospatial information is part of daily monitoring activities, such as UNITAR’s UNOSAT programme that has been supporting the humanitarian community with analysis derived from satellite imagery. This is also helping the work UNESCO carries out in the Middle East region, including efforts to report on the looting of cultural artefacts. The World Heritage Committee has called upon States Parties to use satellite imagery to monitor the state of conservation of World Heritage properties. For example, results have already been reported on a number of sites facing imminent threats, ranging from wildﬁres and sea-level rise to armed conﬂict, including The Historic Centre of Odesa in Ukraine, Baalbek and Tyre in Lebanon, Pantanal Conservation Area in Brazil and Noel Kempff Mercado National Park in Bolivia.
Geospatial Resources UNESCO is sharing its geospatial tools for educational planning on free open-source platforms such as UNESDOC (for reports), QGIS (for plugins), GitLab (for codes) and HDX (for data).

74 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) Geospatial Activities The United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) promotes inclusive and sustainable industrialization, innovation and resilient infrastructure in support of the 2030 Agenda and Sustainable Development Goal 9 (SDG 9).
Within this mandate, UNIDO applies geospatial technologies to map and analyse industrial ecosystems, supply chains and infrastructure resilience.
Through its collaboration with UNITAR–UNOSAT , UNIDO has employed satellite imagery and geospatial damage-assessment mapping to support post-crisis industrial recovery, most notably for the Gaza Industrial Estate and surrounding industrial facilities.
In 2025, UNIDO launched the Compass Platform, a digital mapping system displaying its global projects, ﬁeld ofﬁces and results, further embedding geospatial intelligence into programme management, transparency and results-based reporting. Featured projects on the platform demonstrate UNIDO’s use of satellite, drone and geographic information system (GIS) technologies in industrial and environmental initiatives. In Namibia, the Promoting Sustainable Bush-Processing Value Chains project applied satellite and drone imagery with machine learning to map invasive Acacia bush, estimate biomass and guide sustainable harvesting for charcoal and feed production. In Venezuela, the Industrial Upgrading and Modernization Programme used drone and satellite monitoring of maize crops to assess plant health and soil conditions, enabling targeted fertilizer application and improved yields.
These efforts strengthen UNIDO’s capacity to integrate spatial analysis into industrial policy, crisis response and digital transformation strategies across its Member States.
Geospatial Data and Technology UNIDO’s Compass Platform serves as a centralized geospatial data interface. It visualises the organization’s project portfolios and thematic focus areas, integrating statistical indicators from the UNIDO Statistics Portal.
Replacing the former Open Data Portal, the platform enables users to explore industrial data geographically, ﬁlter results by region or thematic area and access programmatic insights.
In ﬁeld operations, UNIDO leverages satellite imagery and geospatial analysis products, such as those developed by UNOSAT’s Emergency Mapping Service, to assess industrial infrastructure, monitor damage and inform reconstruction planning.
Industrial, energy and environmental datasets collected through technical cooperation projects and Member State reporting are increasingly being georeferenced or spatially visualised to support evidence-based policymaking.
Geospatial Usage UNIDO’s geospatial applications extend across several domains:  Industrial Resilience and Crisis Response: Spatial mapping of industrial zones and facilities supports damage assessments, business-continuity planning and resilient recovery in disaster-affected regions.  Programme Monitoring and Transparency: The Compass Platform enables Member States and partners to visualise project coverage and outcomes, strengthening accountability and knowledge sharing.  Sustainable Value Chains and Eco-Industrial Parks: Mapping industrial clusters, logistics corridors and eco-industrial parks is increasingly reﬂected in UNIDO’s digitalization and circular-economy strategies.  Policy Support and Member State Advisory: Spatially enabled datasets enhance industrial diagnostics, infrastructure planning and the monitoring of SDG 9 indicators. 75 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES Geospatial Resources  UNIDO Mandate and Network: Provides institutional context, including UNIDO’s global ﬁeld operations and their role in applying geospatial approaches.  UNOSAT Collaboration: Offers satellite imagery and rapid-mapping services for industrial-recovery planning.  Compass Platform: Interactive geospatial map and analytics portal showcasing UNIDO’s programmes, projects and ofﬁces worldwide.  UNIDO Statistics Portal: Comprehensive database of industrial and trade indicators suitable for geospatial integration.  Regional Outlook Reports: Highlight industrial hubs, clusters and digital-transformation initiatives with spatial dimensions.

76 BLUEPRINT 2.0 GEOSPATIAL LANDSCAPE OF THE UNITED NATIONS SYSTEM Universal Postal Union (UPU) Geospatial Activities The global postal sector is navigating a signiﬁcant transformation, transitioning from its traditional mail delivery roots towards a dynamic, technologically driven ecosystem. This shift is underpinned by the use of digital technologies to enhance inclusion, improve sustainability and foster collaboration across the sector. The future of postal services is envisioned to be highly integrated within the digital economy, marked by advanced operational efﬁciencies, customer-centric services and a signiﬁcant contribution to societal and environmental goals.
The Universal Postal Union (UPU) works to advance a sustainable and inclusive postal sector, by supporting the digital transformation of postal operators to improve access to basic services for all, including guaranteed postal services. As part of its development policies, the integration and use of geospatial technologies within the postal sector is also included. Some examples are:  Supporting Member States in integrating geographic information system (GIS), satellite imagery and geospatial databases into postal addressing to better identify delivery points and collecting addresses and postcode data in a universal database to optimize operations, enhance efﬁciency and improve service delivery, from dynamic routing to customer service platforms.  Leveraging the global network of over 650,000 post ofﬁces for digital inclusion through the Connect Post initiative, which equips post ofﬁces with high-speed internet, digital training capabilities and the capacity to deliver essential digital services such as e-government, especially to underconnected rural and remote populations.  Gathering information and detecting major corridors of drug trafﬁcking and dangerous goods in international postal trafﬁc, and developing tools to identify parcels likely to contain dangerous goods, using machine learning and artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) trained on current and historical data to generate real-time risk scores.  Maintaining the UPU GIS database of postal events, which holds essential datasets to the organization’s work, such as international ﬁnancial systems, the customs declaration system, the world’s largest database of ofﬁcial postage stamps, or the Express Mail Service system.  Providing support on preparedness and disaster risk management to postal personnel and participating in the joint Global Initiative on AI for Natural Disaster Management  Delivering GIS training to Member States to enhance geospatial skills across its members while promoting the digitalization of the postal sector.  Leveraging international postal, aviation and trade data in a consolidated, AI-enhanced Uniﬁed Data Platform to enable a more accurate statistical measurement of cross-border e-commerce ﬂows and the impacts of logistical constraints, while contributing to the effective decarbonization of international logistics.  Fostering sustainable practices in the postal sector, from green logistics to eco-friendly packaging and promoting social and ﬁnancial inclusion for economic progress. Geospatial Data and Technology Geospatial work within UPU, as transversal infrastructure, is relatively new. To date, a variety of open-source and proprietary tools have been used by different programmes on an ad hoc basis. However, understanding and responding to the evolving postal environment requires accessible and reliable interconnected data. For this reason, the UPU is developing a transversal GIS infrastructure, in cooperation with other UN agencies, to support the use of a mapping platform, satellite imagery and geospatial analysis. UPU’s datasets integrating geospatial information vary in form and nature and comprise information on:  Standardized and interoperable postal address information, integrating administrative boundaries (levels 1 and 2) and postcodes of Member States;  Postal network mapping and service delivery levels, allowing cross-border mail track and trace, routing optimization and delivery efﬁciency;  Greenhouse gas emissions mapping; and  Postal dangerous goods search tool. 77 SPECIALIZED AGENCIES Geospatial Usage The integration of geospatial data and technology within UPU would support the optimal functioning of the international postal service supply chain and the smooth exchange of electronic data throughout the interna tional supply chain, facilitating a seamless experience for postal operators and customers worldwide. This effort is based on the need for greater coherence in the application and sharing of geospatial postal data to manage and measure the cross-border postal network activities, to better contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
At UPU, some examples include address data collection and management for efﬁcient delivery of mail and parcels, route optimization, network planning, postal assets management, postal service planning, based on customer needs and service demand, performance monitoring based on universal service obligation, delivery times, satisfaction and quality of service indicators, e-commerce and monitor the carbon footprint of the postal sector.
